Field surveys of Lampanyctus macdonaldi in the Southern Ocean have provided key insights into its early life history. Newly hatched prolarvae emerge from pelagic eggs at an extremely small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.000014 grams [Wwb = 0.000014 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter reported for several congeneric species. This minuscule starting mass necessitates a rapid transition through the yolk-sac larval stage, during which the endotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The first feeding stage is a critical bottleneck, as the larva must successfully capture its first prey to avoid the point of no return. Following this trophic switch, the free-swimming larva enters a period of rapid growth in the planktonic environment. Observations indicate that individuals attain a standard length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal maturation and the transition to the sub-adult phase. This relatively small size at maturity reflects the species adaptation to a cold, low-productivity environment where early reproductive investment may be favored. The prolonged pelagic larval duration of this myctophid is a defining feature of its life history, influencing recruitment dynamics across its geographic range.

Under the persistently cold conditions of its deep-sea habitat, typically at a temperature of 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C], the reproductive biology of Lampanyctus macdonaldi follows a slow-paced strategy. Females of this rakery beaconlamp produce a modest number of offspring per spawning event, laying approximately 416 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 416 eggs per clutch], which is a relatively low fecundity for a myctophid of its size. This limited clutch size is offset by an extended spawning season, with individuals producing about one clutch per year [F_R_i = about one clutch per year], a pattern that may be linked to the seasonal availability of zooplanktonic prey in the mesopelagic zone. The combination of a small clutch and an annual reproductive cycle suggests that maternal investment per offspring is comparatively high, likely to enhance larval survival in the food-limited waters of the high latitudes. This reproductive mode contrasts markedly with the high-fecundity, low-investment strategy seen in many tropical lanternfishes. The constraints imposed by the thermal regime appear to set a ceiling on the rate at which females can channel resources into gamete production, a finding that aligns with general metabolic theory.

The maximum recorded longevity for Lampanyctus macdonaldi in its natural environment is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] at 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C], a lifespan that is notably extended for a teleost of its modest body dimensions. This extended life history is characteristic of deep-sea fishes inhabiting cold, stable thermal regimes where metabolic rates are suppressed and senescence is delayed. As individuals approach the terminal phase of their life cycle, they attain an ultimate standard length of 16 centimeters [Li = 16 centimeters], a dimension that represents the maximum achievable body size for the species. This asymptotic length is reached gradually over several years, reflecting a slow growth trajectory that is typical of mesopelagic planktivores. The ultimate body size is closely tied to lifetime reproductive output, and in this species, the combination of a decade-long reproductive lifespan and annual spawning events may allow for a considerable total fecundity despite the modest per-event output. The long juvenile period preceding maturity suggests that selective pressures favor somatic durability and late reproduction over a rapid life cycle.

Growth trajectory analyses of this myctophid reveal a pattern of steady mass accumulation from the larval stage to adulthood. The wet weight at puberty, recorded at 3.4 grams [Wwp = 3.4 grams], represents a critical threshold marking the shift from somatic growth toward the initiation of gametogenesis. Individuals at this mass have typically completed the allometric shifts associated with larval metamorphosis and assumed the adult body plan, including fin ray ossification and scale formation. By the time they cease growing, adult specimens reach an ultimate wet weight of 30.6 grams [Wwi = 30.6 grams], a figure that aligns well with allometric predictions based on the standard length of the species. The tenfold increase in mass from puberty to asymptotic size underscores the substantial energetic investment required for post-maturation somatic growth in a food-limited environment. This gradual mass gain is supported by a diet dominated by small copepods and euphausiids, which are seasonally abundant in the mesopelagic zone. The body condition of mature adults fluctuates with prey availability, but the species maintains a relatively stable lipid reserve compared to more migratory myctophids.

Comparative studies among Southern Ocean myctophids highlight the distinctive life-history profile of Lampanyctus macdonaldi. At a water temperature of 5.2 °C [T = 5.2 °C], its maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a daily spawning regime, with females releasing approximately 416 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 416 eggs per day], totaling about 152,000 eggs per year. This high-frequency spawning strategy, while lower in per-event output than many tropical congeners, is compensated by extended longevity and the gradual attainment of a large adult body size. The standard length at puberty of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes delayed maturation in favor of continued growth, thereby increasing fecundity at advanced ages. Field data suggest that body size at first reproduction may vary along a latitudinal gradient, with faster growth rates observed in warmer, more productive waters north of the Polar Front. The ultimate wet weight of 30.6 grams [Wwi = 30.6 grams] represents an upper bound on body mass that appears to be constrained by gill surface area limitations in cold, oxygen-rich waters. Future work should examine how ongoing ocean warming may alter these developmental milestones and reproductive schedules.
